notes.meaning: Benjamin marched out from Gibeah and defeated Israel a second time, striking down eighteen thousand soldiers. Even though Israel was fighting for a just cause and had asked God for direction, doing what was right was still very costly and difficult. God allowed this second loss to humble the people and show them not to depend on their large numbers.

Crushed by this second disaster, the whole assembly of Israel went up to Bethel and wept before the Lord. They fasted, going without food until evening to focus on seeking God, and offered sacrifices to ask for His favor and pardon for their sins. They finally realized that their own pride had kept them from receiving God's blessing.

The ark of the covenant, the sacred chest representing God's presence, was temporarily at Bethel, where Aaron's grandson Phinehas served as high priest. Israel humbly asked whether they should fight their brother tribe again or stop completely, showing they were ready to obey whatever God chose. Because the people genuinely humbled themselves, the Lord promised to give them victory the very next day.

Israel prepared a surprise attack by placing hidden soldiers around Gibeah. Even though God had promised them victory, they still used careful planning and military skill rather than acting carelessly. Their plan was very much like the ambush Joshua had used long before at Ai.

On the third day of battle, the Israelites marched toward Gibeah just as they had done twice before. They set their battle lines in plain view outside the town. This was done to make the Benjamites think another easy victory was ahead.

The Benjamite fighters rushed out of the city and began striking down Israelites on the main roads leading toward Bethel and Gibeah. Benjamin assumed they were winning again, but the Israelites were pretending to run away on purpose. This counterfeit retreat drew the defenders away from their protected city into open ground.

The main body of Israel regrouped and drew up their battle line at Baal-tamar. At the same time, the hidden troops burst out from their positions near Gibeah to strike. The trap had been sprung, catching the Benjamites between two forces.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this chapter as a combination of two separate accounts and consider part of this verse to be an early editorial addition.

notes.meaning: Ten thousand picked Israelite soldiers launched a direct assault against Gibeah, and the fighting grew fierce. The Benjamites fought hard without realizing that total disaster had caught up with them. The Lord gave Israel the victory, and more than twenty-five thousand Benjamite soldiers fell that day.

The Benjamites finally realized they were defeated when the trap snapped shut behind them. Israel had retreated earlier only because they were counting on their hidden troops to take the city. The men in ambush rushed into unprotected Gibeah and put everyone inside to death with the sword.

Israel had prearranged a signal with the ambush force: when the city was taken, they were to send up a massive column of smoke. Benjamin had killed about thirty Israelites and thought they were winning again, just like before. But when they looked back and saw their entire city going up in smoke, they knew all hope was gone.

Seeing the smoke rise, the retreating Israelites spun around and attacked the Benjamites with full strength. The men of Benjamin panicked in terror because they saw that ruin had trapped them on all sides. Their brief triumph quickly turned to horror.

The Benjamites turned to flee toward the wilderness, but the battle swept right over them. Israelite soldiers coming out from the nearby towns joined the fight to cut off their escape. Israel surrounded the fleeing men and easily defeated them east of Gibeah.

Eighteen thousand brave Benjamite soldiers died in the main battle. The survivors broke and ran toward the rocky heights of Rimmon in the wilderness. The Israelites hunted down five thousand more on the roads and another two thousand at Gidom.

A total of twenty-five thousand Benjamite soldiers fell that day, all of them brave fighters. This figure gives a round total for the twenty-five thousand one hundred slain in this final battle. Stubborn rebellion against God had brought a whole tribe to ruin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest verses 45 and 46 were added by a later editor who calculated the total from the casualty numbers mentioned earlier.

notes.meaning: Only six hundred Benjamite men managed to escape into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. They stayed hidden in those mountain caves for four months until the anger cooled and peace could be made. God preserved this tiny remnant so that the tribe of Benjamin was not wiped out entirely.

The Israelites then turned back against the remaining territory of Benjamin, putting all the towns to the sword. They wiped out men, women, children, and livestock, and set fire to every settlement in their path. Their fierce revenge treated their own brothers like condemned Canaanites, showing how destructive their anger had become.
